before: A struct is a value type that can hold fields and methods. Assigning a struct variable normally copies its field values instead of making both variables name one shared object.
new Position() starts its integer field at zero in this simple definition. After assigning X, copying first to second copies that integer. Updating second.X leaves first.X unchanged.
If a struct field itself contains a reference, copying the struct copies that reference, not the referenced object. This example deliberately uses only an int field.
Expected behavior from this example: 2 then 9. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Add an integer Y field and check which fields copy when you assign the struct. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A struct is a value type that can contain fields and methods. This Position struct contains one whole-number field named X.
With this simple definition, new Position() starts X at zero. The next assignment sets first.X to 2.
Assigning first to second copies the struct's field values. Each variable then holds its own X value.
The program prints 2, then 9. Only second.X changes to 9; first.X stays 2.
Copying a struct copies its fields. If a field holds a reference to another object, that reference is copied too; the object it points to can remain shared. This example uses only an int.
